english: Adjusts the game's color, fog, shadows and draw distances on top of the video menu. Everything here is yours alone: in multiplayer each player picks their own, and the server doesn't need the mod.
Turns every setting on these pages on or off. Off is the plain vanilla game.

Sets the Color, Atmosphere, Film and Dynamic grading rows below together. Natural adds a little contrast, color and warmth, thins the grey haze and uses gentle dynamic grading. Cinematic uses filmic tonemapping with a warm tint, a film finish and full dynamic grading. Changing any of those rows by hand switches this to Custom.

Hold this key in game to see the vanilla look and shadows, including the film finish and dynamic grading, and let go to see yours again. Draw distances stay as they are, since reloading trees and grass would stutter. Home by default.
Color grading, applied on top of the game's own.

How bright light is squeezed into what a screen can show. Vanilla keeps the game's curve. Neutral keeps colors true with softer highlights. ACES is the filmic curve many games use: richer and more contrasty, slightly darker. The video menu's Brightness only bends the vanilla curve, so with the others this adds the matching exposure instead.
Brightens or darkens the whole picture, in stops: +1 is twice as bright.
Added to the game's color saturation. Negative values wash colors out.
Positive values warm the picture toward orange; negative values cool it toward blue.
Multiplies every color. White leaves the picture alone.
The fog the game sets for each biome, weather and time of day, scaled and tinted.
How thick the fog is compared to vanilla. Lower values clear the grey haze and show more of the distance; 0% removes it.
Multiplies the fog color. White leaves it alone.
These go past the video menu's limits. Higher values cost frame rate and video memory.
How far away the sun casts shadows. The video menu tops out at 300 m. Close shadows stay as sharp; far ones are softer.
The size of the sun's shadow map. The video menu tops out at 4096. 8192 gives the sharpest shadow edges, especially with a long shadow distance, and uses about 256 MB of video memory.
Small, sharp shadows where things touch the ground and each other, so objects don't look like they float. The game has them at the higher shadow qualities.
Video menu: on at the High shadow quality and above, as in vanilla. On: also at the lower qualities.
How far contact shadows reach, compared to vanilla. Longer ones ground things better but can show halos around thin objects.
These go past the video menu's limits. Higher values cost frame rate.

How far away models switch to their simpler versions, on top of the video menu's Object Quality. Higher values push the switch further out, so less pops in. At 300% trees keep their full models far enough out that they no longer change shape as you walk up to them; lower it for more frames.
Draws trees further out than the game normally does, in rings of 128 m around you.
How far away grass is drawn. The video menu's Grass Distance tops out at about 112 m.
Forces 16x anisotropic filtering on every texture, so ground and walls seen at a shallow angle stay crisp. It costs a little frame rate on older graphics cards.
A camera-like finish on top of the color grading.
Darkens the edges of the screen slightly, drawing the eye to the middle.
Fine black and white grain, mostly in the darker parts of the picture.
How strongly bright lights and the sky glow, compared to vanilla. If Bloom is off in the video menu, it stays off.

Shifts the look by itself with the time of day, the weather and the Blood Moon, blending smoothly. Time of day and weather fade the more enclosed you are, so a lit room at night doesn't turn blue. It never brightens the night.
Warm, golden light around sunrise and sunset, and cool, muted moonlight at night. 0% turns it off.
Greyer and flatter in rain and storms, colder in snow. 0% turns it off.
While the Blood Moon is up: a red tint, harsher contrast and thicker red fog. 0% turns it off.

Rain soaks into everything open to the sky and snow settles on top of it, building up while it falls and wearing off after. Anything under a roof stays dry. Only drawn while something is wet or snowy.

Ground, roofs and roads turn darker and glossy in the rain, reflecting the sky and lights, with a light sheen on walls. They soak through in about a minute of heavy rain and dry over about five minutes.
How much of the flat ground puddles can cover once it's soaked. They ripple while it rains and are the last to dry.

Snow settles on roofs, roads, cars and the tops of blocks during snowfall: the flattest tops first, then gentle slopes as it deepens, with a fine grain that sparkles in the sun. Full cover takes about three minutes of heavy snow, and it melts over about ten.

Real shafts of sunlight and moonlight through windows, doorways, trees and ruins, made from the game's own shadows, and fog that drifts in banks through the valleys and over water when the time and weather bring it. Lamps and torches are Torch's job, so only the sun and moon cast beams.
How finely the air is worked out. Low is the cheapest and a little grainy, High the smoothest. Off turns sunbeams and height fog off.
How bright the beams are. They're brightest looking towards the sun and take its color, gold at dusk. They reach as far as the game draws the sun's shadows.
Dusty air when you're indoors, so beams through windows and holes in the roof really show.

Fog that lies in the low ground and over water in drifting banks, wisps rising off its top, thinning with height so hilltops stay clear. A clear afternoon has next to none: it gathers through the night, is thickest at dawn, and comes with rain, snow, overcast skies and the Blood Moon. It takes the game's fog color.
How much mist gathers in the low ground after dark: it builds through the night, is thickest at dawn, holds for 90 minutes and burns off over the next hour.

Far hills, trees and buildings soften into the color of the air the further away they are, so the land has depth, while everything within about 150 m stays crisp. On a clear day the air takes the sky's hue, blue by day and warm at sunrise and sunset, greying under cloud, rain and snow, with a warm glow towards the sun. The sky itself is left as it is.

How thick the haze is. At 100%, something a kilometer away keeps about three quarters of its own color, and the edge of the view under half. It thins with height and thickens in rain and snow. 0% turns it off.
Small, slow movement that makes the world feel alive: things drifting in the air.

Pollen drifts in the forest air by day, dust in the desert and wasteland, ash in the burnt forest and ice crystals in the snow on clear days, glinting where the sun catches them, and now and then a leaf tumbles down from the broadleaf trees nearby. None of it comes in rain or snowfall. Higher values bring more of them; 0% turns it off.

A new look for lakes, rivers and pools: clear in the shallows and deep blue-green further down, bending what's under it, reflecting the sky and shore, with the sun's glint, foam along the edges and rings when it rains. Far-off water stays the game's own.

Medium reflects the sky and what's around you from the game's reflection probe (Video menu reflections). High also traces reflections across the screen, so shorelines, trees and buildings reflect where they really are; it costs a little more. Off keeps the game's water.
How rough the surface is. Higher makes bigger, choppier waves and more foam; 0% is a still mirror.
Photoscanned ground textures, sharper far-off hills, and the ground keeping its full textures further out.

How much shape far hills keep and how far out the ground keeps its full textures before switching to the blurry far-away version. High doubles that distance and halves the simplification; Ultra goes further and costs more. Game leaves it to the video menu's terrain quality.

Photoscanned replaces most of the game's ground textures with real photographed rock, soil, gravel, asphalt and snow from Poly Haven (free, CC0), each matched to the game's own texture in color and detail so every biome keeps its look. Needs the texture pack in the mod's Resources folder and about 400 MB more video memory. Game keeps the game's own.

Draws the trees past the tree distance too, out to the horizon, as lightweight pictures of the game's own trees taken when a world loads, so far hills are wooded instead of bare. They take the game's sunlight, fog and haze, and give way to the real trees where the game draws them. Off leaves far hills bare, as the game does.

Bushes, plants and many props swap to simpler models as they get further away, and the shader they're drawn with can't blend one model into the next, so every swap is a visible pop as you move. Further moves those swaps out to twice the distance, where they're much harder to spot, for a small cost in frame rate. Game leaves them where the game puts them. Trees blend between their models already and aren't changed.

How far out towns and buildings show, as the game's own simplified versions of them. Default keeps the game's Dynamic Mesh distance (1 km unless changed); 2 km and 3 km put more of them on the horizon, for a little more work for the graphics card.

Past the shadow distance the game has no shadows at all. This lets hills and ridges shade the land, trees and buildings behind them out to the horizon, worked out from the shape of the land, so far valleys darken at sunrise and sunset. It costs little: only the far part of the picture is worked out. Off leaves the far land unshadowed, as the game does.

The game only grows grass on the chunks it has loaded, so past about 100 to 190 m (with the view distance) the ground goes bare and grass pops in as you walk. This draws grass on the far ground too, out to 300 or 500 m, thinning towards the edge, by biome, and not on roads, water, buildings or steep slopes, so the ground stays covered and the game's own grass takes over where it loads. Off leaves the far ground bare, as the game does.
